title: Contrast is not a number
deck: A ratio can pass an audit and still tire the reader. Notes on setting type on dark backgrounds.
body:
We have become accustomed to measuring everything.

Brightness has its values. Darkness has its limits. Contrast has its ratios. And somewhere along the way, we began to believe that understanding something meant being able to assign a number to it.

In digital design, contrast is often treated as a mathematical relationship between two colours. We measure the difference between the foreground and background, compare the results against accessibility standards, and decide whether the combination works.

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) recommend a minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. These figures are important. They establish a baseline for making content accessible.

But meeting a numerical requirement does not automatically make something comfortable to read.

Contrast is not simply about how different two colours are. It is about how they exist together, and how that relationship is experienced.

## Pure White Is Too Much Light

White text on a pure black background produces a contrast ratio of 21:1, the highest possible under the WCAG contrast formula.

Technically, that is excellent. Visually, however, it is not always the most comfortable experience.

On a bright screen in a dim room, pure white can feel unnecessarily intense. Thin letter strokes may appear to glow against the darkness, creating an effect that some readers experience as glare.

The solution is not necessarily to reduce contrast until the text becomes difficult to read. It is to find a more balanced relationship between the foreground and the background.

An off-white text colour against a near-black background with a subtle blue undertone can retain a strong contrast ratio while creating a softer visual experience.

The difference may seem insignificant when viewed as individual colour values, but it can change how an entire page feels.

## Weight Changes With the Ground

Typography does not exist independently of its surroundings.

Light text on a dark background often appears slightly heavier than the same text weight displayed dark on white. Heavy font weights can make small letter spaces and counters feel crowded, while extremely thin weights can appear unstable or shimmer against dark surfaces.

This is why choosing typography for a dark interface requires more than selecting a font and adjusting its size.

A regular font weight, tested at the actual reading size, often provides a more comfortable balance.

The objective is not to make every letter stand out as much as possible. It is to make reading feel effortless.

>A ratio tells you whether text can be read. It cannot tell you whether anyone will want to keep reading.

## Darkness Gives Light Its Meaning

Consider a single light source in two different environments.

In a brightly illuminated room, it might go unnoticed. Place that same light source in complete darkness, and suddenly it becomes the centre of attention.

The light itself has not necessarily changed. Its surroundings have.

This is the interesting thing about contrast. Its meaning is often determined by what exists around it.

A similar principle applies to digital design. A colour that feels balanced on a white background may become overwhelming on a dark one. An accent that appears subtle in one environment might dominate everything in another.

Contrast is contextual. It depends on the surrounding colours, the visual hierarchy, the intended atmosphere and the person experiencing it.

We can measure the difference between two colours, but we cannot reduce the entire visual experience to that measurement.

## Accents Need Their Own Check

Accent colours deserve the same attention as body text.

A saturated colour that works beautifully against white may appear harsh or visually distracting against a dark background. Rather than abandoning the colour entirely, adjusting its saturation and lightness can help it sit more comfortably within the interface.

It is also important to test accent colours in different contexts.

A colour used for a small text link has different requirements from the same colour used as a button background with dark text placed over it.

For example, the amber used on this website, "#e9b96e", provides a strong contrast against its near-black background. It can serve as an accent without becoming visually disconnected from the rest of the design.

The important thing is to evaluate each combination independently rather than assuming that one successful colour pairing makes every other pairing accessible.

## A Short Checklist

Before publishing a dark interface, spend time experiencing it rather than simply inspecting its colour values.

Read an entire article on your phone at night. Read it again during the day, preferably near a window. Pay attention to how the text feels, whether the typography remains comfortable and whether accent colours compete with the content.

Check the contrast ratios, but do not stop there.

If reading feels uncomfortable, begin by adjusting the background and text colours. Then consider the font weight, size and spacing.

Accessibility is not just about passing a numerical requirement. It is about making sure people can comfortably experience what you have created.

## Beyond the Numbers

Two colours can produce the same contrast ratio and communicate entirely different feelings.

One combination might feel peaceful. Another might feel unsettling. One might draw attention to something important, while another might make the entire interface feel overwhelming.

The numbers can be identical, but the experiences are not.

Perhaps this is where we need to reconsider how we approach contrast.

Measurement gives us a starting point. Accessibility gives us a standard. Design gives us the opportunity to go further.

Because sometimes, the best visual decision is not the one that produces the highest number.

It is the one that makes someone comfortable enough to stay.

>Contrast is not a number. It is a relationship.

title: The hundred millisecond rule
deck: Why 100 ms, 1 second and 10 seconds still describe how interfaces feel, and what they mean for your budget.
body:
In his 1993 book *Usability Engineering*, Jakob Nielsen distilled decades of human-factors research into three response-time limits. These numbers are not arbitrary engineering targets. They are rooted in how human perception and attention actually work, which is why they have barely shifted even as hardware has become orders of magnitude faster.

≈ 0.1 seconds (100 ms) feels instantaneous. The user experiences the system as responding immediately. Their flow of thought continues unbroken.

≈ 1 second keeps the user’s train of thought intact. They notice a short delay, but it does not break concentration or make them wonder whether the system is still working.

≈ 10 seconds is roughly the limit before attention wanders. Beyond this, users start looking elsewhere, switching tasks, or abandoning the interaction.

These thresholds come from cognitive psychology and human-computer interaction studies that predate the web. The 100 ms figure, in particular, aligns with the approximate time it takes for a visual stimulus to travel from the retina to conscious awareness in the brain. When a system responds inside that window, it feels like an extension of the user’s own action rather than a separate process.

## What the browser measures now

Google’s Core Web Vitals translated part of this perceptual reality into a concrete metric. In March 2024, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) replaced First Input Delay as the primary responsiveness signal. INP measures the full time from a user interaction (tap, click, key press) until the browser paints the next visual update.

A page is considered good when its INP is 200 milliseconds or less at the 75th percentile of real-user visits, and poor when it exceeds 500 milliseconds.

Notice the gap: Nielsen’s “instant” threshold is 100 ms, while the official “good” mark is 200 ms. That difference matters. The 200 ms figure is a page-level pass mark that accounts for the full variety of interactions and devices. It is not the target for any single control that needs to feel immediate. Treat 200 ms as the absolute ceiling for acceptable responsiveness, and 100 ms as the budget for interactions that should feel instantaneous (button presses, toggles, immediate visual feedback, etc.).

## Spend the 100 ms budget on purpose
When a tap or click must feel instant, you have roughly 100 milliseconds for everything: receiving the input, updating state, performing layout, and painting the result. Anything that cannot fit inside that window needs to be deferred or hidden behind visible feedback that appears within the first 100 ms.

Work out the budget before writing the handler:

1.Input handling and event processing
2.State updates and business logic
3.DOM changes and layout
4.Paint and composite

Put network requests, heavy computation, or rendering of long lists after the first visual response. Show a spinner, a skeleton, an optimistic update, or a subtle state change inside the 100 ms window so the user knows the system heard them.

A simple diagnostic sketch:

```javascript
const t0 = performance.now();
render(items);
requestAnimationFrame(() => {
  const ms = performance.now() - t0;
  if (ms > 100) console.warn('render took ' + Math.round(ms) + ' ms');
});
```

This only measures up to the next animation frame, so it under-reports the full cost of paint and compositing. For the complete picture, open the Performance panel in your browser’s developer tools, record a trace while interacting on a mid-range phone, and inspect the main-thread timeline. Look specifically at the time from input event to the next paint

## Measure first, then argue

Most debates about “is this fast enough?” collapse once someone records a real trace. Build on a powerful laptop and the numbers look fine. Test on a mid-range Android device with a realistic network and the same interaction can easily exceed 300–400 ms. Keep the 100 ms and 200 ms budgets visible to the whole team—on a dashboard, in pull-request templates, or as a standing item in design reviews. When the budget is visible, trade-offs become concrete instead of philosophical.

The hundred-millisecond rule is not a performance slogan. It is a perceptual boundary. Systems that respect it feel responsive and trustworthy. Systems that ignore it feel sluggish even when the underlying hardware is fast. In low-light interfaces, where visual processing is already slower and more effortful, staying inside that window becomes even more important.

title: Write the empty state first
deck: The first screen anyone sees has no data in it. Design that one before the others.
body:
Every list, tracker and dashboard begins empty. Most teams design that state last, if at all, and the result is a blank rectangle with a spinner or a single gray sentence. It is also the one screen every new user is certain to see.

## Three jobs

A good empty state does three things. It says what belongs here. It shows how to add the first item. And it hints at what the screen will look like once it is full.

Compare “Nothing to show” with “No invoices yet. Add one and it appears here with its due date and status.” The second version names the object, offers a next step and previews the result in a single line.

> An empty screen is a promise about the full one.

## Use real examples

When a tool is only for the person who opens it, a few clearly labeled sample rows can teach the layout faster than any copy. Label them as examples and make them easy to clear. When many people will fill the list, keep it honest and leave it empty, but give the empty state the same care as a full one.

## Order of work

Sketch the empty state first, then the single-item state, then the full one. Problems with layout tend to show up in the first two, and they cost very little to fix there.

title: The sixty-five character line
deck: Robert Bringhurst put the ideal line at 66 characters. In CSS you can ask for it directly.
body:
In *The Elements of Typographic Style*, Robert Bringhurst calls a line of 45 to 75 characters satisfactory for a single-column page and 66 characters ideal. Much longer, and the eye struggles to find the start of the next line. Much shorter, and sentences break into fragments.

## Ask for it in ch

The `ch` unit equals the width of the zero in the current font, so a measure set in `ch` scales with the type.

```css
.prose {
  max-width: 65ch;
  line-height: 1.6;
}
```

Because the zero is wider than the average lowercase letter in most faces, a 65ch box tends to hold slightly more than 65 characters of running text. If your face runs narrow, lower the number a little and look at the result.

## Line height follows line length

A longer line needs more space between lines, so the eye can find its way back. Body text at 1.5 to 1.6 works for a 65-character measure. Shorten the line for a sidebar or a caption and the leading can tighten with it.

## On small screens

Phones solve the problem for you, since a 360 pixel viewport at normal body size holds about 40 characters. The risk is on wide monitors, where an unconstrained paragraph can run past 150. Set the maximum, and leave the minimum alone.

title: Shipping less
deck: Notes on removing a feature, and what the quiet afterward teaches.
body:
Most of the work I am proud of this year is work I deleted.

A settings page lost half its toggles. A dashboard lost two charts nobody could explain. A form lost a field that existed because one customer asked for it in 2019.

At first, removing something can feel like moving backwards. We are accustomed to measuring progress by what we add: new features, additional options, more functionality. But sometimes, the best improvement is the decision to stop doing more.

There is something strangely satisfying about removing a feature that no longer belongs. The product remains, but the experience becomes a little quieter. Fewer decisions, fewer distractions, and less unnecessary complexity.

And then comes the silence.

## Every Option Is a Promise

Every feature you introduce comes with a responsibility. It needs to keep working, be documented, and be tested against every feature that arrives afterwards.

The cost of that promise grows quietly. A seemingly harmless button can eventually require maintenance, additional testing, compatibility adjustments, and explanations for people who encounter it for the first time.

That cost is often paid by whoever touches the code next.

A feature does not become valuable simply because it exists. Sometimes, it remains in a product because nobody has questioned its purpose in a long time.

There is also a temptation to preserve things because someone once requested them. A customer needed a particular field several years ago, so it stays. A chart was introduced to make a dashboard more informative, so it remains even when nobody understands what it communicates.

Over time, products accumulate these small decisions. Eventually, the experience becomes less about what people actually need and more about everything that has ever been added.

## How to Decide What Stays

Removing a feature should not be an impulsive decision. Something that appears unnecessary to one person might be essential to someone else.

Before cutting something, I ask three questions.

Who used it in the last ninety days?

What do they do instead when it is gone?

What would we build if we were starting today?

The first question helps establish whether the feature still has an audience. The second reveals whether removing it would create a genuine problem or simply encourage a different way of working. The third is perhaps the most important because it removes the influence of history.

If the answer to the third question looks nothing like the existing feature, then perhaps the feature has outlived its usefulness.

This is where simplicity becomes intentional. It is not about making something smaller just for the sake of minimalism. It is about keeping what serves a purpose and having the confidence to remove what does not.

## The Value of What Remains

Deleting code is the one refactor that almost always makes the next change cheaper.

There is less to maintain, fewer interactions to consider, and less existing behaviour to work around. The product becomes easier to understand, and future improvements have fewer unnecessary obstacles.

But the work does not end with the deletion.

After the cut, write a short note explaining what changed and why. People forgive a removal they understand much faster than one they discover on their own.

It is important to acknowledge that something has disappeared, explain the reasoning behind it, and give people enough context to understand the decision.

Perhaps this is the part we overlook most often. Removing something is not simply about making space. It is about making a deliberate choice about what deserves to occupy that space.

## The Silence Afterwards

When a feature disappears, there is often a brief period of adjustment. People look for what is no longer there. They question whether something has broken or whether the option has simply moved.

Eventually, they adapt.

The empty space begins to feel natural. The interface becomes less demanding, and the product starts to communicate more clearly.

Not every empty space needs to be filled. A screen does not need to occupy every corner, and an application does not need to provide an answer to every possible inconvenience.

There is a particular kind of maturity in knowing when to stop adding.

We celebrate new features because they give us something visible to show. But there is another kind of progress that is much quieter. It does not arrive with a new button or a redesigned interface. Sometimes, it is simply the absence of something that was getting in the way.

And perhaps that is enough.

title: AFTERFRAMES
deck: A Journal of Photography, Memory and Visual Storytelling
body:
>Afterframes is a visual storytelling and photography journal dedicated to exploring the world through images.

It is built around a simple idea: photographs are more than frozen moments. They are fragments of experiences, records of emotions, reflections of society, and windows into lives we may never fully understand.

Every photograph has a story, even when that story is not immediately obvious. A picture of an empty street might remind someone of childhood. A photograph of an elderly person might communicate decades of experience without a single written word. A picture of a sunset might represent the end of a difficult day or the beginning of something new.

Afterframes exists to explore these stories.

It looks beyond the technical aspects of photography, such as camera settings, composition, exposure, and editing. Instead, it considers the emotional, artistic, cultural, and philosophical dimensions of visual imagery.

From the beauty of ordinary surroundings to the complexity of human expressions, Afterframes examines how photographs influence the way we remember, interpret, and experience the world.

It is a place for people who appreciate photography not simply because an image looks beautiful, but because it makes them stop, think, remember, or feel something.

## The philosophy behind the name

![A man in a photolab](/media/Fotolab.png)
There is the story behind the person being photographed, the environment surrounding the subject, the circumstances that created the moment, and the emotions that the image awakens in someone viewing it years later.

The word *Afterframes* captures this idea. It represents the thoughts, memories, interpretations, and emotions that remain after we have looked at an image.

It also reflects the relationship between photography and time. A photograph might capture a moment that lasted only a fraction of a second, yet its meaning can survive for decades.

In that sense, Afterframes is not just about what a camera captures. It is about what remains afterwards.

## What Afterframes explores

The publication will focus on several interconnected areas of photography and visual culture. Each area provides opportunities for thoughtful articles, visual essays, photographic collections, and discussions.

>A. Street photography: Stories hidden in everyday life

Street photography is one of the most fascinating ways of documenting human existence. It captures people in their natural environments, often without preparation or artificial arrangements.

A crowded marketplace, a stranger waiting for a bus, children playing in the street, or someone walking alone under the rain can become powerful photographic subjects.

Afterframes explores the beauty of these ordinary situations and examines how everyday environments can communicate larger ideas about society, identity, loneliness, happiness, and human connection.

>B. Portrait photography: The stories behind faces

A portrait is more than a representation of someone's physical appearance. It is an opportunity to explore personality, identity, emotion, and individuality.

A facial expression can communicate uncertainty, confidence, sadness, happiness, or experiences that cannot easily be explained through words.

This section explores the relationship between people and photography, including how lighting, expressions, perspective, and composition influence the way we perceive individuals.

>C. Nostalgia and memories: Photography as a time machine

One of photography's greatest abilities is its relationship with memory.

A photograph can bring back an experience that happened many years ago. It can preserve the appearance of someone who is no longer around or remind us of a place that no longer exists.

This section explores nostalgia, forgotten places, old photographs, personal histories, and the emotional relationship between images and time.

It also examines how photographs influence our memories and why certain images become more meaningful as we grow older.

>D. Nature and landscapes: Finding beauty in the world

Nature provides an endless collection of photographic possibilities.

From dramatic mountain ranges and quiet forests to oceans, clouds, and changing seasons, the natural world offers countless ways to explore light, colour, atmosphere, and perspective.

Afterframes approaches landscape photography as more than the documentation of beautiful locations. It explores how natural environments influence human emotions and how photographers communicate the scale and beauty of the world around us.

>E. Light, shadows and composition: The language of photography

Light is one of the most important elements in photography. It determines how subjects appear, how colours are perceived, and how an image communicates its atmosphere.

Shadows can introduce mystery. Natural light can create warmth. Harsh lighting can communicate tension, while soft lighting can make an image feel peaceful.

This section examines the artistic techniques behind compelling photographs and how photographers use visual elements to communicate ideas.

>F. Architecture and forgotten spaces

Buildings and physical spaces often tell stories about the people who designed, constructed, occupied, and eventually abandoned them.

Architecture photography provides an opportunity to examine history, culture, design, urban development, and the relationship between humans and their surroundings.

From abandoned structures to modern architectural masterpieces, this section explores the stories that buildings preserve.

title: The Beauty of Being Unnoticed

Finding meaning in the moments the world barely sees.

There is something quietly beautiful about being unnoticed.

In a world where almost everyone is trying to be seen, recognised, remembered, or understood, there is a certain freedom in simply existing without attracting attention. Not every moment needs an audience. Not every experience needs to be documented, and not every beautiful thing needs someone to acknowledge its beauty.

Sometimes, the most meaningful moments happen when nobody is paying attention.

A stranger waiting for a bus. An old man watching the afternoon disappear through his window. Someone walking home beneath the fading evening light. A woman sitting alone in a restaurant, lost in thoughts that nobody else will ever know.

These moments are ordinary to everyone else. But look a little closer, and they begin to tell stories.

Photography has a particular relationship with these unnoticed moments. It allows us to pause where everyone else continues walking. It gives attention to things that would otherwise disappear into the background of everyday life.

And perhaps that is one of the most beautiful things a photograph can do: remind us that something does not have to be important to the world to be meaningful.

We move through life surrounded by thousands of small details, yet we rarely stop to acknowledge them.

We pass people every day without knowing their names. We walk through streets without remembering the buildings. We sit beside strangers without wondering what brought them there.

Our attention is constantly occupied by something else. We are thinking about where we need to go, what we need to accomplish, who we need to meet, and what comes next.

In the process, we overlook the present.

Consider an ordinary afternoon in a city. People are rushing to work, cars are moving through traffic, shops are opening and closing, and conversations are happening everywhere. Somewhere in that activity, a man stands beneath a tree, watching the sunlight move across the pavement.

Nobody notices him.

To most people, he is simply another person occupying a small part of the street. But to a photographer, he might become the subject of an extraordinary image.

Not because he is doing anything unusual, but because the moment itself deserves attention.

The beauty of unnoticed things comes from their refusal to demand attention. They exist quietly, without performance or expectation.

Photography teaches us to recognise that quiet existence.

There is a difference between being alone and being unnoticed.

Being alone describes the absence of company. Being unnoticed describes the absence of attention.

You can be surrounded by hundreds of people and still experience the feeling of being completely invisible. You can also sit alone in a quiet room and feel entirely comfortable with your existence.

The beauty of being unnoticed is not necessarily about loneliness. It is about the freedom to exist without constantly having to explain yourself.

Think about how people behave when they know they are being watched. Their posture changes. Their expressions become more deliberate. They become conscious of how they appear to others.

But when nobody is paying attention, something different happens.

People become natural.

A person laughs without considering whether the laughter is attractive. Someone dances alone in their room. A child becomes completely absorbed in playing. An elderly woman watches the rain without needing to share the experience with anyone.

These are moments without an audience.

And because photography can preserve such moments, it becomes a way of appreciating people without requiring them to perform for the camera.

There is something deeply human about that.

Photography is often described as the art of capturing light, but it is equally an art of paying attention.

A camera does not automatically make something interesting. The photographer's ability to recognise an interesting moment is what gives an image its meaning.

Two people can stand in exactly the same location, looking at the same scene, and produce entirely different photographs.

One might photograph the architecture. Another might notice the shadow of a passing stranger. Someone else might recognise the relationship between the light, the movement, and the person standing quietly in the background.

The difference is attention.

Photographers such as Henri Cartier-Bresson built much of their photographic philosophy around recognising fleeting moments in everyday life. His idea of the decisive moment demonstrated how an ordinary scene could become extraordinary through timing, composition, and observation.

Similarly, Vivian Maier photographed ordinary people, city streets, reflections, and fragments of everyday existence. Much of her work was discovered after her death, giving her photographs another layer of meaning: she had spent years observing the world, often without the world knowing she was doing so.

Their work reminds us that photography does not always need spectacular subjects.

Sometimes, all it needs is someone willing to look.

One of the most interesting things about photographing strangers is that we rarely know their stories.

We might photograph someone walking through a train station, but we do not know where they are going. We might capture a tired expression on someone's face, but we cannot know what happened before that moment.

We see the photograph, but not the entire life behind it.

And that is precisely what makes these images fascinating.

A photograph of a stranger becomes an invitation to imagine.

Perhaps the person is returning home after a long day. Perhaps they are travelling to somewhere they have never been. Perhaps they have just received wonderful news, or perhaps they are carrying something they have not told anyone about.

The image does not provide these answers.

Instead, it leaves room for curiosity.

There is a particular beauty in photographs that do not explain everything. They allow viewers to bring their own experiences, emotions, and interpretations into the image.

A stranger becomes more than a background figure. They become a reminder that every person we encounter has an entire world existing beyond our knowledge.

However, photographing strangers also comes with responsibility. Their anonymity should not be treated as permission to disregard their dignity or privacy. Good street photography observes humanity without reducing people to objects.

A cup sitting beside an open window.

The shadow of a chair against a wall.

A bicycle leaning against an old building.

A curtain moving gently in the afternoon breeze.

The final light of the day touching the side of an ordinary house.

These things are not necessarily rare. In fact, their familiarity is part of their appeal.

We have probably encountered thousands of similar scenes without giving them much thought.

Photography changes the way we relate to these experiences. It encourages us to recognise beauty in places we might otherwise consider unremarkable.

The image becomes less about identifying a person and more about experiencing a feeling.

A silhouette standing beneath a streetlight might communicate loneliness without showing a facial expression. A blurred figure disappearing into a crowd might represent isolation. Someone standing behind a window might suggest distance, separation, or longing.

Anonymity gives photographs room to breathe.

It allows the viewer to imagine themselves in the scene.

Perhaps the person in the photograph reminds you of someone you once knew. Perhaps their posture resembles a moment in your own life. Perhaps the photograph communicates an emotion you have experienced but never quite found the words to describe.

Looking is something we do constantly. Seeing requires attention.

You can walk through the same neighbourhood every morning for five years and still fail to notice the way sunlight enters a particular building at 8 a.m.

You can walk past a beautiful arrangement of shadows without recognising that it will never look exactly the same again.

Photography encourages a different relationship with familiar environments.

Instead of constantly searching for something impressive, you begin observing what is already there.

You notice the contrast between old and new buildings. You pay attention to reflections in shop windows. You observe how people interact with their surroundings. You begin recognising patterns, textures, colours, and moments of stillness.

There is an interesting contradiction in photography.

We take photographs because we want to preserve something, yet many photographs are never shown to anyone.

They remain in folders, buried among thousands of other images. Some are forgotten. Others are rediscovered years later, when the photographer has almost forgotten the circumstances in which they were taken.

But does that make them meaningless?

Not necessarily.

A photograph does not need thousands of views, comments, or recognition to have value.

Sometimes, its entire purpose is to remind one person of a moment that mattered to them.

An image of an empty street might remind someone of their childhood neighbourhood. A photograph of a stranger might recall a particular afternoon. A picture of sunlight entering a room might bring back memories of a place they can no longer visit.

The value of a photograph is not always measured by how many people see it.

Sometimes, it is measured by what it allows one person to remember.

And perhaps that is the ultimate beauty of being unnoticed.

Not everything meaningful needs to become visible to the world.

An observer does not always need to be part of the scene.

They can stand at a distance and appreciate the way things unfold. They can recognise beauty without needing to possess it. They can witness a moment without making themselves the centre of it.

This approach requires patience.

You might spend an hour in one location and take only three photographs. You might wait for the light to change, for a person to enter the frame, or for two unrelated elements to align in an interesting way.

You might even leave without taking a photograph.

And that is perfectly fine.

Not every moment needs to become an image. Sometimes, the act of noticing is enough.

The camera should not become a reason to stop experiencing life. Instead, it should become another way of experiencing it.

Perhaps we have spent too much time looking for beauty in the foreground.

We look for the main subject, the most interesting person, the brightest colour, or the most dramatic part of a scene.

But the background often contains its own story.

The person walking behind the main subject. The empty building across the road. The window reflecting a different world. The shadow that quietly connects two unrelated objects.

These details might initially appear unimportant, but they can completely change how a photograph feels.

A person standing in front of a large building can communicate scale. A tiny figure surrounded by an enormous landscape can communicate vulnerability or freedom. An empty chair in the background can suggest that someone was recently there.

The background is not always just a place where the main subject exists.

Sometimes, it is the story itself.

Learning to photograph unnoticed things means learning to give these overlooked details the attention they deserve.

Perhaps we do not always need to be noticed.

Perhaps there is beauty in walking through a city without anyone knowing our name. In sitting quietly somewhere and watching life happen. In experiencing something wonderful without immediately reaching for a camera or thinking about how to share it.

The world is full of stories that will never be told, faces that will never be recognised, and moments that will never be remembered by anyone except the people who experienced them.

Photography cannot preserve everything. It cannot tell us the complete story of a stranger, recreate the exact feeling of a particular afternoon, or prevent time from moving forward.

But it can give us something else.

It can remind us to pay attention.

To look beyond the obvious. To appreciate the ordinary. To recognise that the world does not become beautiful only when something extraordinary happens.

Sometimes, beauty is simply a person existing quietly in a world that has not stopped to notice them.

And sometimes, that is more than enough.
